CT417 Topic Guide

CI/CD and Git Workflows

Turn a delivery failure in a company scenario into concrete Git, CI, test, image and deployment steps.

What repeatedly appears in the papers

CI/CD is a major recent question family: 2023/24 asks for CI advantages and adoption pitfalls; 2024/25 asks for pipeline improvements, Git commands and GitHub Actions YAML; 2025/26 asks for a Docker deployment diagnosis, pipeline design, release risks and merge-conflict handling. Expect a 20-mark scenario with several practical subparts.

Rapid refresher

Problem in a scenarioAnswer withWhy
Late or conflicting integrationShort-lived branches, pull requests, protected main, CI on every PRSmall changes are tested before they destabilise the shared branch.
Manual or weak testingBuild, unit/integration/regression tests, coverage reportsGives fast, repeatable feedback.
Production-only failureVersioned artefact, staging parity, smoke tests, controlled release and rollbackTests the same build in a realistic environment and enables recovery.
Late security discoverySAST, dependency/secret checks and image scanning in CIMoves security feedback before release.

How to answer

  1. For every stated failure, give one named pipeline control.
  2. Say where it runs: pull request, merge to main, staging or production.
  3. Explain the benefit in terms of the scenario, not as a generic definition.
  4. For commands or YAML, preserve the order and identify the branch/tag being acted on.

Practice question - delivery and Git workflow (20 marks)

Inspired by: 2024/25 Question 1 and 2025/26 Question 1.

Scenario. ParcelPilot releases a Node.js service weekly. Tests are mainly manual, feature branches conflict when merged late, staging differs from production, and a deployment fails with manifest for registry.example/pilot/api:latest not found.

(a) Recommend four CI/CD improvements for ParcelPilot. Link each to a stated problem. [8 marks]

Model answer: (1) Run build, unit and integration tests on every pull request, replacing late manual feedback. (2) Require review and a passing CI status before merging short-lived feature branches into protected main, reducing conflict and unstable integration. (3) Build a versioned Docker image once, deploy that version to production-like staging, and run regression/smoke tests there; this detects environment differences before production. (4) Add SAST, dependency and secret checks to CI, with a defined gate for serious findings; this finds vulnerable code or libraries before release. Keep a previous version available for rollback.

(b) Using Git and basic Docker commands, show how you would diagnose, identify and fix the manifest error. [5 marks]

Answer route: first confirm what tag the workflow is trying to pull; then inspect which tags were pushed; finally build/push the missing version or change deployment to the version that exists.

git log --oneline -5
git status
docker pull registry.example/pilot/api:latest
docker image ls
docker build -t registry.example/pilot/api:<commit-or-version> .
docker push registry.example/pilot/api:<commit-or-version>
docker pull registry.example/pilot/api:<commit-or-version>

Model answer: The log confirms that the registry has no latest manifest, usually because the build job did not push it or the deploy job uses a different tag. Build and push a versioned tag, then deploy that same tag. A good answer does not claim that docker pull repairs a missing manifest.

(c) Outline the stages of a GitHub Actions pipeline that tests pull requests, then builds/pushes an image and deploys to staging after merge to main. [4 marks]

Model answer: On pull_request: checkout, install dependencies, run tests and fast checks, publish results. On a push to main: checkout the merged commit, build/test, create and push a versioned Docker image, deploy that exact version to staging, then smoke-test and publish deployment status. Production promotion should be separate and recoverable.

(d) Explain how merge conflicts arise and give a practical prevention/resolution process. [3 marks]

Model answer: A conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically combine incompatible edits, commonly when two branches change the same lines or one deletes code another edits. Rebase or merge main into the feature branch regularly; keep branches small; use pull-request review. When a conflict occurs, inspect the markers, choose or combine the intended code, run tests, stage the resolved files, commit, and complete the merge/rebase. Never resolve by blindly accepting one side.

Final check

  • Did I attach each recommendation to an explicit scenario failure?
  • Did I distinguish a PR trigger from a merge-to-main trigger?
  • Did I name the exact image version rather than rely on an unexplained latest tag?
